q: In what year was the Federal Reserve Act enacted?
explain: The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 created the Federal Reserve System and gave it responsibility for setting monetary policy.

sources.title: The Fed - Federal Open Market Committee
sources.quote: The Federal Reserve Act of 1913 gave the Federal Reserve responsibility for setting monetary policy.

sources.title: Federal Reserve System | Britannica
sources.quote: The system was created by the Federal Reserve Act , which President Woodrow Wilson signed into law on December 23, 1913.

q: How many regional Federal Reserve Banks are there?
explain: The Federal Reserve System includes 12 regional Federal Reserve Banks alongside the Board of Governors and the FOMC.

sources.title: Federal Reserve System | Britannica
sources.quote: It consists of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, the 12 Federal Reserve banks, the Federal Open Market Committee, and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB)

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Discount Window
sources.quote: The twelve Reserve Banks operate the discount window and work together to ensure consistent and effective operations across the Federal Reserve System.

q: How many members sit on the Federal Reserve Board of Governors?
explain: The Board of Governors has seven members, all of whom are also voting members of the FOMC.
hook: Seven governors, seven days a week.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Board Members
sources.quote: The seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

sources.title: Federal Reserve System | Britannica
sources.quote: The seven-member Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System determines the reserve requirements of the member banks within statutory limits

q: How long is a full term for a member of the Fed's Board of Governors?
explain: A full Board term is fourteen years, which insulates governors from short-term political pressure.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Board Members
sources.quote: A full term is fourteen years.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: Based in Washington, D.C., and serving 14-year terms, the Governors are a federal agency representing different sectors of the economy and different geographic regions across the country.

q: How long is the term of the Chair of the Federal Reserve Board?
explain: The Chair, Vice Chair and Vice Chair for Supervision are nominated by the President from among the governors, confirmed by the Senate, and serve four-year terms.
hook: Chair term = 4 years; Board term = 14 years.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Board Members
sources.quote: The Chairman and the Vice Chair of the Board, as well as the Vice Chair for Supervision, are nominated by the President from among the members and are confirmed by the Senate. They serve a term of four years.

sources.title: Federal Reserve System | Britannica
sources.quote: The Chairman of the Board of Governors is appointed to a four-year term by the president of the United States .

q: Which chamber of Congress confirms nominees to the Fed's Board of Governors?
explain: Governors are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Board Members
sources.quote: The seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System are nominated by the President and confirmed by the Senate.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: Led by the Federal Reserve Chair, these members are nominated by the President of the United States and confirmed by the Senate.

q: Can a Fed governor who has served a full term be reappointed?
explain: A member who serves a full term may not be reappointed, but a member who completes an unexpired portion of a term may be.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Board Members
sources.quote: A member who serves a full term may not be reappointed. A member who completes an unexpired portion of a term may be reappointed.

q: How many voting members does the Federal Open Market Committee have?
explain: The FOMC's 12 voting members are the seven governors, the New York Fed president and four rotating Reserve Bank presidents.

sources.title: The Fed - Federal Open Market Committee
sources.quote: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) consists of twelve members--the seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; and four of the remaining eleven Reserve Bank presidents, who serve one-year terms on a rotating basis.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: Its 12 members include seven Fed board governors, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York , and four of the remaining 11 Fed bank presidents, who enter and exit the FOMC on a rotating basis.

q: The president of which regional Reserve Bank is a permanent voting member of the FOMC?
accept: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
explain: The New York Fed president always votes; the New York Fed carries out the FOMC's open market operations.
hook: New York runs the trading desk, so New York always votes.

sources.title: The Fed - Federal Open Market Committee
sources.quote: The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) consists of twelve members--the seven members of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York; and four of the remaining eleven Reserve Bank presidents, who serve one-year terms on a rotating basis.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: The New York Fed bank president is always a voting member in the FOMC. That's because the NY Fed carries out the FOMC's open market operations (OMOs)--buying or selling securities to help steer interest rates as directed.

q: How many of the eleven non-New York Reserve Bank presidents vote on the FOMC in a given year?
explain: Four of the remaining eleven Reserve Bank presidents vote, each serving a one-year term on a rotating basis; non-voting presidents still attend and participate in discussions.

sources.title: The Fed - Federal Open Market Committee
sources.quote: four of the remaining eleven Reserve Bank presidents, who serve one-year terms on a rotating basis.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: All the Fed bank presidents participate in FOMC discussions and economic and policy assessments (think of it as a policy debate before the actual vote), but only four reserve bank presidents participate in the voting process. Each serves for one year on a rotating basis.

q: Which Reserve Bank shares an FOMC rotation group with only Chicago?
explain: The rotating seats come from four groups: Boston, Philadelphia and Richmond; Cleveland and Chicago; Atlanta, St. Louis and Dallas; and Minneapolis, Kansas City and San Francisco.
hook: The two Great Lakes Feds - Cleveland and Chicago - share a seat.

sources.title: The Fed - Federal Open Market Committee
sources.quote: The rotating seats are filled from the following four groups of Banks, one Bank president from each group: Boston, Philadelphia, and Richmond; Cleveland and Chicago; Atlanta, St. Louis, and Dallas; and Minneapolis, Kansas City, and San Francisco.

q: How many regularly scheduled meetings does the FOMC hold each year?
explain: The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings per year, roughly six weeks apart, and can also meet unscheduled when needed.
hook: Eight meetings, about every six weeks.

sources.title: The Fed - Federal Open Market Committee
sources.quote: The FOMC holds eight regularly scheduled meetings per year.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: The FOMC meets eight times annually, although the actual dates vary from year to year. The meetings are typically spaced six weeks apart (with a longer break in the summer)

q: Besides stable prices, what is the other goal of the Fed's dual mandate?
explain: Congress assigned the Fed to conduct monetary policy to support maximum employment and stable prices, together known as the dual mandate.

sources.title: The Fed - What economic goals does the Federal Reserve seek to achieve through its monetary policy?
sources.quote: Specifically, Congress has assigned the Fed to conduct the nation's monetary policy to support the goals of maximum employment and stable prices. Those two goals are often referred to as the Fed's "dual mandate."

sources.title: The Federal Reserve's Dual Mandate - Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
sources.quote: Our two goals of price stability and maximum sustainable employment are known collectively as the "dual mandate."

q: Besides maximum employment and stable prices, what third goal does Section 2A of the Federal Reserve Act name?
explain: Section 2A directs the Board and FOMC to promote maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates; the first two are commonly called the dual mandate.
hook: Jobs, prices, and the quiet third: moderate long rates.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Section 2A. Monetary policy objectives
sources.quote: The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Federal Open Market Committee shall maintain long run growth of the monetary and credit aggregates commensurate with the economy's long run potential to increase production, so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement of longer-run goals and policy strategy
sources.quote: The FOMC is firmly committed to fulfilling its statutory mandate from the Congress of promoting maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.

q: In what year did Congress add Section 2A, the monetary policy objectives, to the Federal Reserve Act?
explain: Section 2A was added by an act of November 16, 1977, directing the Board and FOMC to promote maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates.
hook: The mandate arrived in the stagflation '70s.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Section 2A. Monetary policy objectives
sources.quote: [12 USC 225a. As added by act of November 16, 1977 (91 Stat. 1387) and amended by acts of October 27, 1978 (92 Stat. 1897); Aug. 23, 1988 (102 Stat. 1375); and Dec. 27, 2000 (114 Stat. 3028).]

sources.title: The Federal Reserve's Dual Mandate - Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
sources.quote: In 1977, Congress amended the Federal Reserve Act , directing the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Federal Open Market Committee to "maintain long run growth of the monetary and credit aggregates commensurate with the economy's long run potential to increase production, so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices and moderate long-term interest rates."

q: What longer-run annual inflation rate does the FOMC judge most consistent with its price-stability mandate?
explain: The FOMC judges that inflation of 2 percent over the longer run, measured by the annual change in the PCE price index, is most consistent with its mandate.
hook: Two percent - the Fed's North Star.

sources.title: The Fed - Why does the Federal Reserve aim for inflation of 2 percent over the longer run?
sources.quote: the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) judges that inflation of 2 percent over the longer run, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with the Federal Reserve's mandate for maximum

sources.title: The Federal Reserve's Dual Mandate - Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
sources.quote: The Committee judges that inflation at the rate of 2 percent, as measured by the annual change in the Price Index for Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE), is most consistent over the longer run with the Federal Reserve's statutory mandate.

q: Which price index does the FOMC use to define its 2% inflation goal?
explain: The 2 percent goal is measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures (PCE), not the CPI.
hook: Fed targets PCE; headlines quote CPI.

sources.title: The Fed - What economic goals does the Federal Reserve seek to achieve through its monetary policy?
sources.quote: The Federal Open Market Committee judges that an inflation rate of 2 percent over the longer run, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent with the Fed's price-stability mandate.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement of longer-run goals and policy strategy
sources.quote: The Committee judges that inflation at the rate of 2 percent, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent over the longer run with the Federal Reserve's statutory mandate.

q: In what year did the FOMC first issue its Statement on Longer-Run Goals specifying a 2% inflation goal?
explain: The FOMC's statement of longer-run goals and policy strategy, which set the 2 percent PCE inflation goal, was first released on January 25, 2012.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Federal Reserve issues FOMC statement of longer-run goals and policy strategy
sources.quote: The Committee judges that inflation at the rate of 2 percent, as measured by the annual change in the price index for personal consumption expenditures, is most consistent over the longer run with the Federal Reserve's statutory mandate. ... Last Update: January 25, 2012

sources.title: The Federal Reserve's Dual Mandate - Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
sources.quote: The FOMC's longer-run goals were first articulated in its January 25, 2012, press release and have been reaffirmed annually thereafter.

q: In which FOMC publication does the 'dot plot' of policymakers' rate projections appear?
explain: The Summary of Economic Projections includes each policymaker's projection of the appropriate federal funds rate, shown as the dot plot.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: Four times a year, the Fed publishes its Summary of Economic Projections report, which tracks how each Fed member projects future interest rates (see figure 1).

sources.title: The Fed - FAQs (FOMC economic projections)
sources.quote: Specifically, the projections include information about policymakers' projections of the appropriate level of the target federal funds rate--that is, the path that each policymaker judges likely to be most consistent with the Federal Reserve's statutory mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices

q: How many times a year are FOMC economic projections (including the dot plot) published?
explain: Projections are collected four times a year, in connection with the March, June, September and December FOMC meetings.
hook: Dots at the quarter marks: March, June, September, December.

sources.title: The Fed - FAQs (FOMC economic projections)
sources.quote: Economic projections are collected from each member of the Board of Governors and each Federal Reserve Bank president four times a year, in connection with the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC's) meetings in March, June, September, and December.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: Four times a year, the Fed publishes its Summary of Economic Projections report, which tracks how each Fed member projects future interest rates (see figure 1).

q: Which Fed body determines the interest rate on reserve balances (IORB)?
wrong: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
explain: The IORB rate is determined by the Board and is an important tool for the Fed's conduct of monetary policy, supporting the FOMC's federal funds target range.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Interest on Reserve Balances
sources.quote: The interest rate on reserve balances (IORB rate) is determined by the Board and is an important tool for the Federal Reserve's conduct of monetary policy.

q: In an overnight reverse repo (ON RRP) operation, does the Fed initially buy or sell a security?
explain: In an ON RRP the Fed sells a security to an eligible counterparty and agrees to buy it back the next day; it is a supplementary tool to keep the federal funds rate in the target range.
hook: Reverse repo: Fed sells today, buys back tomorrow.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Overnight Reverse Repurchase Agreement Operations
sources.quote: When the Federal Reserve conducts an ON RRP operation, it sells a security to an eligible counterparty and simultaneously agrees to buy the security back the next day.

q: Over what term do depository institutions lend reserve balances to each other at the federal funds rate?
explain: The federal funds rate is the interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Open Market Operations
sources.quote: the federal funds rate--the interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight

sources.title: The Federal Reserve's Dual Mandate - Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago
sources.quote: The federal funds rate is the interest rate these institutions charge when they lend reserves to other institutions overnight.

q: Relative to the FOMC's federal funds target range, where has the discount window primary credit rate been set since March 2020?
wrong: 50 bp above the top of the range
explain: The primary credit rate is set at the top of the FOMC's target range; it is established by each Reserve Bank's board of directors, subject to review and determination by the Board of Governors.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Discount Window
sources.quote: Rate: Since March 2020 the primary credit rate has been set at the top of the target range that the FOMC has set for the federal funds rate. The rate is established by each Reserve Bank's board of directors, subject to the review and determination of the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System.

q: What is the common name for the Fed reducing its asset holdings to shrink its balance sheet?
explain: The FOMC sets the direction for asset purchases (quantitative easing) or asset reductions (quantitative tightening) to influence long-term interest rates.

sources.title: Federal Open Market Committee | Britannica Money
sources.quote: The FOMC sets the direction for asset purchases or asset reductions (quantitative easing and quantitative tightening) to influence long-term interest rates.

q: What does the FOMC view as its primary means of adjusting the stance of monetary policy?
accept: target range for the federal funds rate
explain: In its balance sheet principles the Committee states it views changes in the federal funds target range as its primary policy tool, with balance sheet reduction secondary.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Board - Policy Normalization
sources.quote: The Committee views changes in the target range for the federal funds rate as its primary means of adjusting the stance of monetary policy.

q: Which Fed body is responsible for open market operations?
wrong: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency
explain: The Board of Governors is responsible for the discount rate and reserve requirements, while the FOMC is responsible for open market operations.
hook: Open Market operations - Open Market Committee.

sources.title: The Fed - Federal Open Market Committee
sources.quote: The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System is responsible for the discount rate and reserve requirements, and the Federal Open Market Committee is responsible for open market operations.
